phonemes.desc: Long diphthong αι [ai̯] with acute pitch accent; the alpha is open and the iota forms an off-glide.
Short [da], the middle syllable of the name.
Short [los], the final syllable with a clear liquid l.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DIE-dah-los' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the remaining syllables are short and light.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Δαίδαλος (Daidalos), from δαιδάλλω, 'to work cunningly, to fashion with art' — the name is an adjective made flesh

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Daedalus, the Roman rendering adopted into English

kin.label: Family
kin.form: Father of Ikaros; nephew and victim of Perdix (or Talos); exile from Athens, master-craftsman of Knossos and Sicily

pronunciation.note: The Greek Δαίδαλος contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (the diphthong αι is long), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Daedalus is a secondary spelling that preserves the consonants but obscures the original Greek vowel quantities.

domains.title: The Cunning Craftsman
domains.subtitle: Inventor, Architect, and Wingsmith
domains.lead: Daidalos is the master craftsman of Greek mythology: the architect of the Labyrinth, the maker of moving statues, and the father of Icarus. His name means 'cunningly wrought' and became a byword for any work so skillful that it seemed alive. He is the first engineer in Western literature, the inventor whose ingenuity saves him and destroys those he loves.

cards.name: The Labyrinth
cards.desc: The maze he built at Knossos to contain the Minotaur — so cunning that its maker could barely find the way out (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7-9).

cards.name: Wings
cards.desc: The feathered wings he fashioned from wax and twine to escape Crete — the technology that saves the maker and kills his son (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-235).

cards.name: Automata
cards.desc: The moving statues he made so lifelike that Plato says they had to be chained down lest they walk away (Meno 97d).

cards.name: Invention
cards.desc: The transforming power of human skill, celebrated and feared by the Greeks — every artifact of his works exactly as designed, and every design costs him something.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The instruments of escape and the boundary between human and divine — held together by wax, held up by obedience

symbols.name: Wax
symbols.meaning: The material that holds the wings together and melts when the warning fails — technology as a perishable interface between instruction and desire

symbols.name: Labyrinth
symbols.meaning: The architectural puzzle that embodies his cunning and its dangerous consequences — a mind built in stone

symbols.name: Tools
symbols.meaning: The axe, file, and compass of the craftsman who can make anything except a safe life

symbols.name: The thread
symbols.meaning: The clue Ariadne unrolled through the maze — in Hyginus' telling (Fabulae 43) Daedalus' own stratagem — the one invention designed to be undone

symbols.name: The moving statues
symbols.meaning: His animated figures, so lifelike they had to be tethered — the ancient image of art imitating life one step too far

mythology.lead: The myths of Daidalos are preserved in Homer, Apollodorus, Diodorus, and Ovid: a small cycle that celebrates human invention and prices it — envy, exile, and the fall of a son. Every artifact he makes works exactly as designed, and every design costs him something he did not intend to pay.

myths.title: The Nephew He Killed
myths.text: Daedalus' first recorded act is his worst. His sister entrusted her son to his tutelage — the boy is Perdix in Apollodorus (Library 3.15.8), Talos or Calos in Ovid (Metamorphoses 8.236-259) — and the pupil outshone the master: Perdix invented the saw, taking his cue from a fish's spine or a snake's jaw, and then the potter's wheel and the compass. 'Fearing he might outstrip him,' Ovid writes, Daedalus hurled him from the Acropolis; Athena caught the falling boy and changed him into the partridge — perdix — that still flies low, remembering the fall. Daedalus was banished and fled to Crete. The myth plants its theme at the very root of his career: the first great maker of the Greek imagination is also the first to destroy a rival talent, and the tradition never lets him forget it — the partridge flutters through his story like a conscience.

myths.title: The Labyrinth
myths.text: At the court of Minos, Daedalus built the monument that defines him: the Labyrinth, 'a maze with winding paths, confusing and impassable,' designed to imprison the Minotaur — the bull-headed child born of Pasiphaē and the Cretan bull (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7-9). The maze was so cunning that its maker, Apollodorus says, could barely find the way out. When Theseus came to Crete as tribute, Ariadne fell in love with him and gave him the thread that marked the path through the puzzle — in Hyginus' version (Fabulae 43) the stratagem was Daedalus' own. Plutarch (Theseus 15) preserves the rationalizers' spin: a prison, an ordinary house, a dance-floor — the ancients were already decoding it. The myth's point needs no decoding: the greatest craftsman in Greece builds a structure whose only function is that no one inside it can get out — including, soon enough, its maker.

myths.title: The Wings
myths.text: Minos imprisoned Daedalus and his son Icarus in the Labyrinth — some say a tower — and the inventor answered confinement with flight. He gathered the feathers the gulls left on the shore, sorted them by size, and bound them with thread and wax, shaping two pairs of wings 'like a bird's, but fitted to human shoulders' (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-189). His speech to Icarus is the myth's heart: fly the middle course — too low and the spray wets the feathers, too high and the sun melts the wax; 'take the middle way.' The boy exults and climbs; the wax softens; he falls into the sea that forever bears his name. The sources disagree on the physics — Apollodorus (Epitome 1.11-13) says Icarus flew too low, dazzled by the sun glittering on the waves — but either way the wax is the argument. Daedalus, 'now neither a father nor a son,' reaches Sicily alone: the wings work, and the warning is the first thing that fails.

myths.title: Cocalus and the Death of Minos
myths.text: In Sicily, King Cocalus sheltered the fugitive, and Daedalus repaid him with wonders: the fortified city of Camicus and warm baths, Diodorus reports (4.78-79). Minos came in pursuit, tracing the fugitive by a famous challenge — a great reward to whoever could pass a thread through a spiral seashell. Daedalus solved it by tying silk to an ant; Minos demanded the hand of the solver, and Cocalus' daughters, acting on Daedalus' counsel, scalded the king to death in his bath (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.14-15; Hyginus, Fabulae 43; the shell-trick lives on in the paroemiographers). The tyrant who owned a labyrinth died in a bathroom, undone by a thread and an insect. The episode completes Daedalus' portrait: every pursuit of him ends in a puzzle only he can solve, and every puzzle protects him — his genius is his armor, and it is never enough to make him safe.

myths.title: Things That Almost Live
myths.text: Before the wings, Daedalus was already famous for figures that moved. Homer knows 'the dancing-floor which Daidalos once made for fair-tressed Ariadne in spacious Knossos' (Iliad 18.590-592), and classical tradition credited him with the first statues to open their eyes and part their limbs — Pliny (Natural History 36.13) has him inventing walking statues. Plato gives the thought its sharpest form (Meno 97d): Daedalus' statues are so lifelike that 'if they are not tied down, they run away' — and Socrates jokes that his own arguments need the same tether. The joke contains the whole myth: Daedalus' creations keep escaping their maker's intentions, from the Labyrinth to the wings to the nephew he could not keep from soaring. Ingenuity, in his case, is the art of making things that outrun him — which is why his name became the Greeks' word for anything so skillfully made it seems alive, and so alive it cannot be controlled.

lore.syncretism: The Romans absorbed him as Daedalus, and Ovid's Metamorphoses book 8 — the wings, the fall, the nephew — fixed his canonical Latin form; Virgil alludes to the Cretan maze (Aeneid 5.588-591: 'the Cretan labyrinth... Daedalus, pouring his genius into the craft'). The Renaissance made him the emblem of the artist-engineer, from Vasari's lives to the emblem-books; in the twentieth century James Joyce rebuilt him as Stephen Dedalus, the young artist escaping the nets of family, religion, and nation — wings that also melt. Modern engineering borrowed his name without irony (Project Daedalus, the British Interplanetary Society's interstellar probe study). He remains the myth's permanent consultant on invention: every story about technology outrunning its maker is his story retold.
lore.culturalLegacy: Daedalus is the archetype of the inventor and the artist in one figure — the engineer whose creations work too well. The labyrinth gave European languages its word for any designed confusion; the wings fathered every myth of flight from Icarus to the space program; the moving statues made him the patron, millennia early, of robotics and AI. Modern debates about autonomous systems, from Frankenstein to lethal drones, are his debate: can a maker foresee what his making will do? Homer already knew the answer the tradition keeps giving — the dancing-floor is beautiful, the maze is brilliant, and both outlive the hand that made them.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Daidalos is the first Western portrait of the inventor as tragic hero. His gifts are extraordinary; his judgment is not. He kills his nephew from envy, builds a prison for a monster, and loses his son to the very technology that saved him. Each invention solves one problem and creates another, and the pattern is so consistent that the Greeks made his name an adjective for any cunningly wrought thing.

To meditate on Daidalos is to meditate on the double edge of human making. We are the species that makes wings, and we are the species whose children fly too high. The question the myth hands us is not whether to invent — he will invent, that is what he is — but whether we can learn to give warnings that outlast the wax. The name Daidalos still means 'cunningly wrought'; it still sounds, in Greek, like a compliment and a diagnosis.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Δαίδαλος. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent. The plain ASCII daedalus flattens the diphthong into ae and removes the accent. The PuniCodex restoration Daidalos preserves the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because the diphthong is long and accented.

sources.name: Morris, Daidalos and the Origins of Greek Art (1992)

lore.archaeology: Homer anchors Daedalus in Bronze Age Knossos a thousand years before the classical city-states told his story, and Arthur Evans' excavations (1900-1905) gave the myth a landscape: the palace's corridors, bull-imagery, and wall paintings let moderns walk his labyrinth. Ancient Athens claimed him too — the murder of Perdix was set on the Acropolis — and classical authors (Pliny, Natural History 36.13) credited him with the first true sculpture, 'opening the eyes and separating the limbs.' The Archaic sculptural style of the seventh century BCE is still called 'Daedalic' after him. No secure artifact is his; like the labyrinth, his archaeology is a structure of plausible paths.
